name: Rosa Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Rosa. I work for the Work Futures Panel as a field researcher. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Can you start by walking me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee excavator operator at Greenstone, an open-pit lithium mine, the stuff that goes into car batteries. I load trucks with a 120-tonne digger, which sounds big until you see the trucks. A good day is when I keep the trucks coming without them waiting on me. On a bad day I'm the bottleneck and the dispatcher lets me know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to mining?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fifteen years managing a hardware store for a big chain. I was good at it, but the pay had stopped going anywhere, and I like learning new things. I'm a numbers person, so I worked out the mine would pay forty percent more even as a trainee, and I applied. My husband Marco is a self-employed electrician, and we've got Lucia, who's twelve, and Mateo, who's seven. We've got over a year's expenses saved and some money in an index fund, which is just a cheap way to own a little bit of lots of companies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy getting better every week, it's like a game where I can see my score. I use AI every day: I had one build me a spreadsheet of my load times so I can see where I'm slow. The hard part is the bucket control on a wet bench, I'm still clumsy, and the twelve-hour nights mess with my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, back to work. I'd probably post something like, turns out the robots needed more training than me. I'm not a big believer in hype either way, so I wouldn't be shocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm getting better on the digger every month, and in a slow world the people who keep learning move up. I'd be a fully qualified operator in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: keep tracking my numbers, keep using AI to study for the next ticket. Keep putting money into the index fund every payday. Maybe use the stable years to help Marco grow his business a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You track your own load times. Does the mine know you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor, Kwame, found out and asked for a copy. Now half the trainees want my spreadsheet, and I'm the one who's been here nine months. It's nice being useful while you're still the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you help Marco with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His quoting and invoicing are a mess, it's all in a notebook in the van. I'd set him up with proper software and an AI assistant for quotes. He'd complain for a week and then love it.

S0.say: She'd say fine, back to work, and might joke online that the robots needed more training than she did. She isn't a believer in hype either way.
S0.think: She thinks a slow world favours people who keep learning, and expects to be fully qualified within a year or two.
S0.do: Keeps tracking her load times and using AI to study for her next ticket, adds to the index fund every payday, and helps her husband set up quoting software.
S0.quote: Now half the trainees want my spreadsheet, and I'm the one who's been here nine months.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa treats her trainee role like a game with a scoreboard, and her own AI-built spreadsheet has already made her useful beyond her experience. She's unsentimental about AI either way. Her energy flows easily into side projects like her husband's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be smart about it. At work I'd tell the trainees to learn the systems that run the machines, not just the machines. I wouldn't blame anyone; companies do what makes money, and governments should make sure people get trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Diggers are harder to automate than trucks, so I'd have a bit of time, and I'd use it to jump into the control or planning side. I'm already halfway there with my spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Kwame who runs the fleet management system and ask to shadow them. I'd take an online course in mine planning software in the evenings and pay for it myself if I had to. Within a year I'd want to be in a planning or dispatch role, even if it's a pay cut at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like a moving target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a pay cut. How would that work with a mortgage and two kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be fine for a year or two. We've got the savings and Marco's busy. I'd rather take a ten percent cut now than a hundred percent cut in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, oddly. He's a great supervisor, but he's proud of never touching a computer. I'd try to drag him along with me, but he'd have to want it.

S1.say: She'd tell trainees to learn the systems running the machines, not just the machines, and wouldn't blame anyone: companies chase profit and government should ensure training.
S1.think: She privately thinks she'd be fine, since diggers are harder to automate than trucks, giving her time to move into control or planning work.
S1.do: Asks to shadow the fleet management team in the first month, pays for an evening course in mine planning software, and aims to move into a planning or dispatch role within a year even at a pay cut.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited by the moving target.
S1.quote: I'd rather take a ten percent cut now than a hundred percent cut in three years.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa runs the numbers on her own future the way she ran a hardware store. She'll take a small pay cut now to dodge a bigger loss later. She frames blame in purely practical terms, without heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shake-up and the government will have to step in, because when everyone's affected at once, it stops being a personal problem and becomes a policy problem. I'd say stay calm and look after your money. I wouldn't join protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried but not lost. My job, the planning job and Marco's work all get hit eventually. But robots need installing, charging and wiring, and Marco's an electrician, so there's a gap there for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week I'd sit down with Marco and do the numbers: a year of savings, the index fund, his business. I'd keep my mine job as long as it lasted. Then I'd go into business with Marco installing charging and power for robot fleets at farms and small sites, and I'd do the quoting, ordering and AI side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a lot, but I'd feel like I had a plan by the end of the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does having two years' warning help, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot, actually. Two years is enough to start a business if you've got savings and a husband who can wire anything. It's not enough to retrain properly, but I wouldn't try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer than most people would. Is that real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd have bad nights, and I'd worry about Lucia's schooling. But I managed a store through two recessions. You make a list and you work the list.

S2.say: She'd say the government will have to step in because when everyone's affected it becomes a policy problem, and she'd advise people to stay calm and look after their money.
S2.think: She expects her job and her husband's to be hit eventually, but sees a gap in installing power and charging for robot fleets that his electrical trade could fill.
S2.do: Reviews savings, the index fund and the business with her husband in the first week, keeps her mine job as long as possible, then goes into business with him wiring power for robot fleets while she handles quotes and AI tools.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with bad nights but a plan within the first month.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to start a business if you've got savings and a husband who can wire anything.
S2.fieldNote: Rosa looks for the gap that rapid automation opens rather than the jobs it closes. Her calm comes from experience managing a store through two recessions, and from savings. She admits to bad nights and worry about her daughter, which keeps her answer believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and people should use it. I'd tell my crew to start learning now and stop arguing about whether it's real. I'd want the government to make retraining cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I'd spend two or three years in mine planning, earning well, while building the business with Marco on the side. By 2031 the business could be the main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, move into planning. Years two and three, start the electrical business properly with Marco, nights and weekends. I'd also start putting a bit of the index fund into companies making mining robots, because I'd rather own a piece of what replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AI eventually do the quoting and planning side of the business too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure. I'm not trying to outrun the robot, I'm trying to be the one who sells the robot its electricity. Someone still has to own the van and sign the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia about her own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet. I'd tell her go for it, because animals and people want a person's hands. I'd also tell her to learn the AI tools as she goes, like a second language.

S3.say: She'd call five years fair warning, tell her crew to start learning now instead of arguing, and want government to make retraining cheap.
S3.think: She sees five years as good for her: two or three well-paid years in planning while growing the electrical business into the main income by 2031.
S3.do: Moves into planning in year one, builds the electrical business with her husband on nights and weekends in years two and three, and shifts part of the index fund into mining robot makers.
S3.quote: I'm not trying to outrun the robot, I'm trying to be the one who sells the robot its electricity.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Rosa layers a career step and a business on top of each other. Her line about selling the robot its electricity sums up her approach: own a piece of the change. Her advice to her daughter treats AI as a second language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains in 2035 that they didn't see it coming wasn't paying attention. Maybe I'd put it more kindly than that. I'd tell people to make a plan this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years might be almost too slow for me. I'd get bored waiting. I think I'd make my move earlier than I needed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two years on the digger to get fully qualified, then move into planning. I'd do a part-time business course, then run the electrical business with Marco full-time by year five. I'd pay the mortgage off early, and set aside money for both kids' studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, in fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With so much time, is there anything you'd do differently from the five-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it properly. In five years I'd cut corners to get the business going. With ten I'd get the business course done, hire an apprentice, and maybe open a second van. Ten years turns a survival plan into a proper business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned getting bored. Does that ever get you into trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would say yes. I once rearranged the whole hardware store on a Sunday because I was bored. Head office was not happy. So I'd keep myself on a leash a bit.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty and anyone surprised in 2035 wasn't paying attention, though she'd put it more kindly. She'd tell people to make a plan this year.
S4.think: She thinks ten years might be almost too slow and she'd get bored waiting, so she'd likely move earlier than needed.
S4.do: Gets fully qualified on the digger in two years, moves into planning, takes a part-time business course, runs the electrical business full-time with her husband by year five, pays the mortgage off early and saves for both kids' studies.
S4.quote: Ten years turns a survival plan into a proper business plan.
S4.fieldNote: Rosa is one of the few who treats ten years as almost too much time. The decade lets her build a proper business rather than a survival plan. Her story about rearranging the store out of boredom shows a restless streak she knows to keep in check.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even with a plan, everyone around us would be in trouble at the same time and the kids would feel that. What would help is cheap, short courses that the government actually pays for, and fewer forms for people starting small businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people see opportunity or just loss. Most of the people I work with only see loss, and I get why. I'm not braver than the guys on my crew. I just did the maths on the hardware store and learned it doesn't care how loyal you are.

headlineQuote: I'm not braver than the guys on my crew. I just did the maths on the hardware store and learned it doesn't care how loyal you are.
portrait: Rosa Diaz is a 43-year-old trainee excavator operator at an open-pit lithium mine, who left fifteen years of managing a hardware store because the numbers stopped adding up. She's married to a self-employed electrician, has two kids, a year's savings and an index fund, and uses AI every day, including a spreadsheet she built to track her own load times. She's pragmatic, blames no one and sees change as something to plan around. She stays calm in most scenarios and only uneasy with two-year AGI, where she'd start an electrical business with her husband wiring power for robot fleets.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because even with a plan everyone around them would be in trouble at once and the kids would feel it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, short courses paid for by the government, and fewer forms for people starting small businesses.
